title: Patients' Recovery
text: We have a long history of research into hospital design and patient recovery. A long time ago, people began to study therapeutic environments. For example, in 1855, Florence Nightingale recognized that colour and spatial forms could promote patients’ recovery. She found that grass, fresh air and sunlight had positive effects, and architectural design also played an important role. Views of hospital backyards can help patients rest well and fall asleep more easily, while also relieving their stress and pain because of the pleasant feelings caused by nature. Receiving visits from family and friends helps patients recover sooner, and so does staying in a private single room. Ninety percent of hospital patients and nurses agree that a well-designed hospital environment is associated with higher recovery rates.

title: Internet Growth
text: The rapid expansion of the Internet has revolutionized our lives, influencing both the quality and quantity of interactions and information accessibility. One significant change is in the realm of research. Online research offers several advantages, such as speed, cost-efficiency, and the ability to reach diverse or otherwise inaccessible groups. These features have made it a cornerstone of modern studies and data collection, enabling researchers to gather vast amounts of information quickly. However, this shift to online methods is not without challenges. One major drawback is the lack of face-to-face communication, which eliminates the ability to interpret body language or other non-verbal cues that are essential for understanding context and intent. Additionally, the anonymity of the Internet means researchers cannot always verify the identity of participants, leading to potential issues with data reliability and authenticity. As online research continues to grow, balancing its advantages with strategies to mitigate its shortcomings will be crucial for maintaining the quality and credibility of studies conducted in the digital age.

title: Global Warming
text: There can now be no reasonable, science-based, doubt about the reality of global climate change effects brought on by the cumulative and rapidly growing emission of so-called “greenhouse gases” - primarily carbon dioxide - into the atmosphere. As these effects become increasingly more obvious worldwide, so commercial interests, groups of concerned individuals and national governments have been gripped by what amounts to mass panic about what to do about it. To many, Paul Ehrlich's Malthusian “Population Bomb" of 1968 appears about to explode in the world’s face in an indirect version of his millenarian vision of population growth which outpaces agricultural production capacity - with predictably catastrophic results for humanity. And his three-part crisis scenario does indeed seem now to be present: a rapid rate of change, a limit of some sort, and delays in perceiving that limit. Ehrlich's work was roundly criticized at the time, and later, from many quarters, and much of what he predicted did not come about. Nevertheless, can the world afford to take the risk that the climate scientists have got it wrong? Is it not in everyone's interest to apply the Precautionary Principle in attempting to avoid the worst of their predictions - now, rather than at some future time? As the Chairman of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, Mr. Rajendra Pachauri, has recently pointed out, eleven of the warmest years since instrumental records began have occurred in the past twelve, while major precipitation changes are taking place on a global scale.

title: Negativity Bias
text: Negativity bias refers to the psychological phenomenon where humans tend to focus more on negative emotions or experiences than positive ones. Although we experience positive emotions like contentment and pleasure more frequently, these feelings tend to be lighter in intensity and are less likely to be remembered or linger in our minds. On the other hand, negative emotions such as fear, anger, or sadness, although less frequent, tend to be much stronger and more intense, making them easier to recall and harder to forget. This bias has evolutionary significance. In the past, paying more attention to negative events like threats or dangers would have been advantageous for survival. By being more sensitive to potential threats—whether from predators, environmental hazards, or social conflicts—humans could respond quickly to life-threatening situations. This heightened awareness of negative stimuli would have helped our ancestors make decisions that favored safety and survival. In today's world, while the immediate life-threatening threats may have diminished, the negativity bias still plays a role in how we evaluate the environment and survive, sometimes leading us to focus on potential risks or problems rather than opportunities or positive outcomes. Understanding this bias can help us manage our reactions and potentially shift our focus towards a more balanced perspective.

We feel content and pleasant more frequently, but these positive emotions are lighter, which means they cannot be easily recalled or stay in our minds.

Negativity bias can help us evaluate the environment and survive when we face life-threatening issues.

title: Architecture Design
text: When we are dealing with buildings of the Victorian era or earlier we are looking at a building stock that has already been rid of architectural flops. In a process of natural selection the many thousands of buildings that were built or designed poorly have already fallen down or have already been modified and the faults rectified. So, this is James Wyatt's masterpiece Fonthill Abbey, a building of unquestioned brilliance, historical importance, even genius. It started to fall down, and finally collapsed in 1825, long before listing of buildings was invented or even contemplated. Then even earlier in February 1322, the central tower of Ely Cathedral collapsed. And when it came to reconstructing it, it was decided to build an octagon of stone with a much lighter timber structure on top, a work of genius but not the original intended crowning feature. So, the cathedral we have today has long ago been rid of its design and engineering faults. But when we are dealing with buildings which are only fifty or sixty years old, we are often confronting design flaws or poor workmanship that are only just coming to light, or only just in the process of being rectified. This again challenges our perception of authenticity. Most historic buildings (by which I mean buildings a hundred years or more old) have been adapted and modified to iron out design and construction flaws and so their so-called original state is, in fact, an altered state in which they perform well, in fact often better than when they were first completed. Late twentieth century buildings are still going through this Darwinian process of natural selection that will decide whether they will survive having been adapted or whether they will die being unsuited to their function. So criticizing them for their design flaws may be seen as being rather unfair.

title: Luxury Brand
text: The question today of what makes a luxury brand, a luxury brand and how do we distinguish it, is very hard to answer. The standard business response is to say they are more exclusive. title: Bees and Darwin
text: Worker bees exhibit remarkable altruism, a behavior deeply embedded in their genetic and evolutionary traits. text: I suppose you wouldn't expect perhaps to find a mathematician in a museum of historical objects, but actually, the objects that I've been drawn to in this museum have quite a lot of mathematical significance. title: DNA Pieces
text: My lab works on the applications of synthetic biology, so we're very interested in doing useful things with biological systems. title: Credit Card
text: An experiment on customer behavior explored the impact of messaging strategies on the usage of inactive credit cards. Participants were divided into two groups, each receiving a different type of communication. One group was presented with messages highlighting the benefits they could gain from using their credit cards, such as rewards or cash-back incentives. The other group received messages emphasizing potential penalties or missed opportunities if they failed to use their cards, such as losing loyalty points or account privileges. The findings revealed a significant psychological difference in customer motivation based on the type of message: twice as many people in the second group used their credit cards as in the first group. This suggests that threatening potential losses is more effective than highlighting potential benefits when encouraging customers to take action. Customers who were informed about potential losses exhibited a stronger inclination to activate and use their cards compared to those who were promised gains. This outcome aligns with the well-established concept in behavioral economics known as “loss aversion," which suggests that individuals tend to prioritize avoiding losses over acquiring equivalent gains.

The other group received a message implying a penalty if it is not used.

title: Approach and Avoidance
text: Approach and avoidance motivation is composed of three conceptually distinct components. Approach indicates a propensity to move toward (or maintain contact with) a desired stimulus, such as vocational plans. Avoidance indicates a propensity to move away from (or maintain distance from) an undesired stimulus in order to reduce anxiety. Motivation is defined as the energization and direction of behavior. The valence of stimuli is at the core of the distinction between approach and avoidance, with positively valenced stimuli typically leading to approach and negatively valenced stimuli typically leading to avoidance. Stimuli can be external or internal, implicit or explicit, conscious or non-conscious.

title: Industrial Revolution (Short Version)
text: Through the 1950s and into the 1960s, the idea of the Industrial Revolution was that it was the work of some genius inventors who created machines used primarily in the textile industry — but also in mining — that eliminated blocks to assembly line production. Then everybody was crowded into factories and the new brave world opened up. In fact, one of the most interesting books and great classics that is still in print was written by an economic historian at Harvard who's still around called David Landes. It's a good book called The Unbound Prometheus, which was basically that. Some of the inventions that I briefly describe in your reading, the spinning jenny, etc., refer to that. Well, that kind of analysis led one to concentrate on England, where the Industrial Revolution began, and to view industrialization as being a situation of winners and losers. That analysis has been rejected greatly over the past years, because the Industrial Revolution is measured by more than simply large factories with industrial workers and the number of machines. This is the point of the beginning of this. The more that we look at the Industrial Revolution, the more we see that the Industrial Revolution was first and foremost an intensification of forms of production, of kinds of production that was already there. Thus, we spend more time looking at the intensification of artisanal production, craft production, domestic industry — which we've already mentioned, that is, people, mostly women but also men and children, too, working in the countryside. The rapid rise of industrial production was very much tied to traditional forms of production.
